#82023. What did the Soviet Union's final deep space probe actually see on Mars?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1556 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Space ↗ Open Full Page

What did the Soviet Union's final deep space probe actually see on Mars?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1556 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, on July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket.
  • However, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft.
  • So what caused the odd-looking appearance of the shadow in the final images captured by Phobos 2, and what was the real reason behind the spacecraft's sudden failure?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket. The spacecraft's mission included the study of Mars and the Martian moon Phobos, with a planned close approach and deployment of landing probes, and over the next several months, the spacecraft successfully captured more than three dozen images of Phobos during its time in service.

However, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft. Adding to the mystery were objects in some of the final photographs dispatched by the doomed spacecraft, which seemed to show an elongated shadow beneath the probe — a strange twist in one of the Soviet Union's final space missions, and one that soon gave rise to conspiracy theories about what the fate of Phobos 2 might have been.

So what caused the odd-looking appearance of the shadow in the final images captured by Phobos 2, and what was the real reason behind the spacecraft's sudden failure?

Originally, the Soviet Union had planned for Phobos 2 to reach the Red Planet by late January 1989, after which the spacecraft would begin collecting data about the Martian environment leading up to its initial contact with Mars' largest moon in early June.

In a recent development, to say that a lot hinged on the success of the mission would be an understatement, given the unfortunate fate of the probe's predecessor, Phobos 1, which went offline on Sept. 2, 1988, after a faulty command sequence was initiated while the spacecraft was on its way to Mars. The stakes were almost immediately raised as Phobos 2 arrived in orbit around Mars on Jan. 30, 1989, when one of the probe's three onboard flight system processors was found to have gone offline, with another already experiencing technical issues.

In a recent development, over the course of the next several weeks, Phobos 2 was able to overcome some of these setbacks and successfully began sending useful scientific data about the Martian environment back to Earth. By March, all the probe's science instruments appeared to be functioning normally, and despite the earlier loss of one of its processors, the remaining two had continued to facilitate control of the spacecraft by its Soviet ground control team.

That all changed on March 27, 1989, as Phobos 2 prepared to capture navigational images of its namesake as the Martian moon passed, which would be useful in advance of another forthcoming flyby in early April.

Achieving this meant that the probe had to be angled in such a way that it faced Phobos, whereby its communications antennas would be temporarily directed away from Earth. During the imaging portion of the maneuver, all appeared to go smoothly, but soon afterward, ground controllers realized they were unable to reestablish contact with the probe.

Industry observers note that A few fleeting radio contacts were made over the ensuing hours, which engineers believed might indicate that during the period of signal loss required for imagery of Phobos to be obtained, the spacecraft may have begun to spin uncontrollably. If this were the case, and the spacecraft could not reorient its solar panels toward the sun, it would eventually lose all power.

No further contact with Phobos 2 could be established beyond this point, although images from the probe's final close encounter with the Martian moon were successfully delivered back to Soviet ground controllers. While investigators identified a failure involving the spacecraft's onboard computer system as the most probable explanation, to this day, the exact cause of the events leading to the loss remains unknown.

Recent findings suggest that although questions remain about the fate of Phobos 2, several theories have been put forward over the years. According to authors Paolo Ulivi and David M. Harland, one of the simplest explanations was that the spacecraft was damaged after an impact with other material orbiting the Martian moon, although later modeling by Soviet engineers and American teams at NASA's Jet Propulsion Lab seemed to rule this out.

A more likely scenario involved failure of the probe's second attitude control computer, which had already begun experiencing technical issues as Phobos 2 arrived in Martian orbit. With two of its three processors now offline, the third and sole remaining computer was unable to maintain control of the spacecraft on its own. An additional factor might have been power loss from battery drainage while the probe's solar arrays were directed away from the sun, and with no failsafe to power down any non-critical systems under such conditions, the spacecraft would likely have undergone significant power loss.

However, the probe's failure was only one part of the mystery: equally perplexing had been the unusual images Phobos 2 captured in its final moments, which later sparked speculation — and conspiracy theories — about what might have been behind the spacecraft's sudden demise.

In some of the final images captured by Phobos 2, an unusual, elongated shadow had been visible in the frame, which with time would begin to prompt the most unusual of all the theories about the probe's demise: that it had been disabled by an alien spacecraft.

According to recent reports, among the proponents of this theory had been Marina Popovich, a former experimental pilot and the first Soviet woman to break the sound barrier, who set over 100 world aviation records in her career. In 1991, Popovich held a press conference at the Soviet Consulate in San Francisco, where she claimed a cigar-shaped object had been photographed near the Martian moon, which she believed to be an alien mothership.

Sources indicate that given her storied background in Soviet aerospace history, Popovich's views likely carried a degree of credibility unlike most others. However, that did not make them accurate.

Determining what the images actually show requires an understanding of the probe's orbit, particularly with relation to the Martian moon it was attempting to photograph. At the time, the spacecraft and Phobos were in almost the same orbit, and moving at very similar speeds. As Ulivi and Harland note, due to these conditions, the probe's Termoskan multispectral imager often captured images that "included the shadow of the moon on the planet's surface as a dark oblong cigar-shaped feature.".

In 1991, a NASA-led study of the Termoskan observations concluded that the unusual appearance of the shadow most likely resulted from a combination of factors acting together. The study team attributed these to the scanning instrument itself, as well as the spacecraft's near-co-orbital motion with Phobos, its viewing direction, and finally, a slight rocking motion the researchers concluded the spacecraft had likely exhibited at the time.

It has been revealed that however, another factor that contributed to the appearance of the shadow involves the oblique angle at which the moon's shadow strikes the Martian surface. Because of this, similar imagery depicting an elliptical or elongated shadow cast by Phobos has been obtained since the Phobos 2 mission, with examples including images captured by the High-Resolution Stereo Camera (HRSC) on the ESA's Mars Express spacecraft in 2005.

The loss of Phobos 2 became a controversy for reasons other than the imaginative speculations about what its final images might have captured.

John M. Logsdon, director of the Space Policy Institute at George Washington University's School of International Affairs, remarked to the Los Angeles Times shortly after the failure that the situation was "just horrible," noting that the mishap was expected to potentially fuel what he called "a first-rate bureaucratic struggle" the Soviet Union was undergoing amid political changes occurring there at the time.

"The scientific community is also facing challenges resulting from the restructuring of the Soviet system," the Times also reported, noting the scientists from more than a dozen nations around the world whose funding and scientific instruments, at an estimated cost of several millions of dollars, "must be counted among the losers in the failure of the probe to complete its basic mission.".

In a recent development, although both Phobos spacecraft were lost prior to completion of their primary missions, there were still some meaningful scientific results they produced. These included new data collected about both Mars and Phobo­s which, according to Ulivi and Harland, exceeded the total data collected from all past Soviet missions to the Red Planet.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, the circumstances surrounding the demise of Phobos 2 remain one of the more intriguing episodes in the history of Soviet space exploration. The unusual observations made during its final moments, coupled with lingering questions about precisely what went wrong, have helped sustain decades of speculation.

In a recent development, today, the truncated Phobos 2 mission remains a curious ending note for the Soviet-era space program. It is one that still fuels speculation, and reminds us how rapidly the unknown can take our minds to imaginative places — especially when it comes to mysteries involving space, the cosmos, and the potential existence of life beyond Earth.

Industry News: Watch out, AlphaFold: Claude and ChatGPT’s fresh biology skills wow scientists

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, accurately predicting protein structures has been the preserve of specialist AI tools like AlphaFold — but now general-purpose models are catching up.
  • Earlier this month, Xinming Tu set out to test what artificial-intelligence models know about proteins.
  • Recent findings suggest that he left the analysis to run overnight and woke up shocked at the results.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, accurately predicting protein structures has been the preserve of specialist AI tools like AlphaFold — but now general-purpose models are catching up. Credit: EMBL-EBI (CC0).

Earlier this month, Xinming Tu set out to test what artificial-intelligence models know about proteins. Tu, a researcher at an AI biology manufacturer called Phylo in South San Francisco, California, asked large language models (LLMs) from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google to predict the sequences of obscure bacterial proteins.

Recent findings suggest that he left the analysis to run overnight and woke up shocked at the results. The latest versions of Anthropic’s Claude models had outperformed other LLMs — but also specialized ‘protein language models’, which are trained on vast troves of sequence data and specially designed for such tasks.

Scientists are using AI to dream up revolutionary newly introduced proteins.

Scientists are using AI to dream up revolutionary newly introduced proteins.

When Tu and Leo Chen, a computational biologist at Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts, shared the results in a 16 November blogpost, it set off a frenzy among computational biologists to see what other protein biology LLMs such as Claude could do. For instance, Tu and Chen and others have found it could perform a key step in protein-structure prediction.

And on 24 November, OpenAI announced that its latest language models had successfully designed upcoming proteins, some of which behaved as expected when made and tested in the lab. The results hint that the latest LLMs might be gaining a sophisticated understanding of protein biology.

The research has kicked off a debate over the future of biological AI. Some scientists predict that ‘general purpose’ models such as Claude and ChatGPT will eventually outperform specialist tools such as AlphaFold at tasks including protein structure prediction and design.

“We want to see a world where a scientist can just describe in natural language what they want a ChatGPT model to do, and the model can just be infinitely flexible and design exactly what the person wants,” claims Joy Jiao, who leads life-sciences research at OpenAI in San Francisco, California.

But some researchers question the extent to which LLMs are learning underlying lessons in protein biology. They suggest that some of their abilities could be the result of regurgitating training data.

According to recent reports, the release of AlphaFold2, Google DeepMind’s blockbuster protein-structure-prediction AI, in 2020 launched a revolution in biological AI. There is now a vast ecosystem of software — much of it open source — for modelling different properties of proteins, such as how they interact with possible drugs, and for designing upcoming proteins.

Sources indicate that researchers have begun using LLMs to orchestrate these specialist models, but it has mostly been as a time-saving measure, notes Martin Pačesa, a structural biologist at the University of Zurich. “In most cases, a specialist will always perform better than a generalist for a given task,” he says.

Five protein-design questions that still challenge AI.

Five protein-design questions that still challenge AI.

In a recent development, to see if an LLM could stand in for specialist protein-design tools, Jiao and her colleagues asked an OpenAI model called GPT-6.2 to design 3D protein structures capable of binding to five different biological targets, including proteins implicated in cancer and immune disorders. After the LLMs generated the designs, the researchers used a specialist AI tool to determine a corresponding genetic sequence. Lab experiments confirmed that around 11% of designs were able to bind their target.

In other experiments, the OpenAI team indicated that its LLMs could design protein sequences, redesign existing antibodies, and other tasks typically performed by specialist tools. In some cases, the LLM performed as well as some specialist tools, and in others, such as predicting the 3D structure of proteins, it was far off. OpenAI researchers describe the work in a blogpost and technical paper.

Jiao emphasizes that the work is a proof of principle, and that specialized AI tools were still needed for key steps. But Masatoshi Uehara, an OpenAI researcher who was part of the effort, believes that LLMs will only get better at protein biology. “I believe the large language model can technically beat every specialized model in even each capability,” he states.

  • Sources indicate that researchers at Delft University of Technology (The Netherlands) have accomplished something that physicists previously thought should not be possible.
  • Recent findings suggest that the findings, published in Nature Communications, also present scientists with a fresh puzzle.
  • Atoms in magnetic metals such as iron and nickel behave like tiny magnets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that researchers at Delft University of Technology (The Netherlands) have accomplished something that physicists previously thought should not be possible. Using radio waves, they managed to directly control the magnetic spin of the nucleus inside a single atom. The unexpected result challenges existing assumptions about how atomic magnetism behaves and could eventually lead to new ways of storing and retrieving quantum information.

Recent findings suggest that the findings, published in Nature Communications, also present scientists with a fresh puzzle. Although the experiment demonstrated that this remarkable level of control is possible, researchers do not yet fully understand the mechanism that makes it work.

The Hidden Magnetism Inside Every Atom.

Atoms in magnetic metals such as iron and nickel behave like tiny magnets. However, the magnetism within an atom comes from different sources. Both electrons and, in some cases, the atomic nucleus possess a quantum property called spin, which can be thought of as a miniature magnetic compass needle.

"By far the strongest magnetism comes from the electrons," claims lead researcher Sander Otte. "But in some atoms, the nucleus also carries a spin. That spin is much weaker, but it is also much better shielded from the outside world.".

That protection makes nuclear spin especially interesting to quantum researchers. Because it is less exposed to disturbances from its surroundings, it could offer a promising way to preserve delicate quantum information.

To investigate these tiny magnetic properties, Otte's team uses a specially modified scanning tunneling microscope. This powerful instrument allows the researchers to deliver electrical signals to individual atoms with extraordinary precision.

Until recently, their experiments concentrated primarily on electron spin because it is easier to detect and measure. The nucleus's magnetic spin could only be observed indirectly through a phenomenon known as the hyperfine interaction, which creates a subtle quantum connection between the spins of the electron and nucleus. This connection can cause the two spins to become slightly entangled, meaning their quantum states are linked.

An Atomic Experiment Produces an Unexpected Result.

In the latest study, lead author Hester Vennema and her colleagues took a different approach. They simultaneously applied two separate signals to a single atom, with one directed at the electron and the other at the nucleus.

Sources indicate that by using these signals together, the researchers could investigate their effects independently. What happened next caught them by surprise.

Even when the electron and nuclear spins were largely disentangled, the team was still able to flip the orientation of the nucleus's magnetic spin. Based on their previous understanding, the nucleus should not have responded in this way.

"According to our simple understanding, this should not really happen," claims Otte. "The nuclear spin should not be sensitive at all to the electrical signals from a scanning tunneling microscope.".

The result suggests that the interaction between electrical signals and nuclear spin involves a mechanism that scientists have yet to fully explain.

Controlling Quantum Spins Like Guitar Strings.

Recent findings suggest that achieving this level of precision required the researchers to adapt a technique called double magnetic resonance so it could operate on a single atom. The method allowed them to manipulate the magnetic behavior of the atomic nucleus separately from that of an electron.

Magnetic resonance works by applying a wave signal at a carefully selected frequency to change the orientation of a magnetic spin. However, quantum mechanics restricts these changes to specific allowed transitions, meaning the frequency must be precisely matched to the spin being targeted.

Vennema compares the process to playing a musical instrument.

"You can compare it to the strings of a guitar," Vennema explains. "Each possible spin rotation is like a string with its own note. You have to play precisely the right note to make a particular string vibrate. The "notes" of a nuclear spin are a hundred to a thousand times lower than those of an electron spin.".

According to recent reports, in other words, electrons and atomic nuclei respond to very different frequencies, much as different guitar strings produce different musical notes. By tuning their signals to the appropriate frequencies, the scientists could address the two types of spin separately.

A Quantum Breakthrough With a Mystery Still to Solve.

Sources indicate that the discovery could have important implications for the future of quantum information technology. Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum systems can use quantum states to encode information in more complex ways.

Recent findings suggest that one major challenge is keeping those states stable long enough for information to be stored and retrieved reliably. Nuclear spins are attractive candidates for quantum memory because they are relatively well isolated from environmental interference.

Recent findings suggest that the ability to control these spins directly could therefore open new possibilities for writing, storing, and reading quantum information. However, the findings represent an early experimental advance rather than a ready-to-use quantum memory technology.

Industry observers note that for now, one of the most notable outcomes is the upcoming scientific mystery the experiment has revealed. The researchers have demonstrated an unexpected way to manipulate nuclear spin, but the physical mechanism responsible remains unclear.

"Back to the drawing board, then," states Otte. "That is really how science works. There is always something fresh left to figure out.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that when does Cameron Diaz not sound like Cameron Diaz?
  • For more than 30 years, whenever the Oscar-winning actor has appeared on German screens, she has spoken with the voice of Katrin Fröhlich.
  • Sources indicate that the same goes for all other famous actors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when does Cameron Diaz not sound like Cameron Diaz? When you're in a German cinema.

For more than 30 years, whenever the Oscar-winning actor has appeared on German screens, she has spoken with the voice of Katrin Fröhlich.

Sources indicate that the same goes for all other famous actors. In Germany's €125-million ($138-million) voiceover industry, Hollywood's up-and-comers are "adopted" by a voice actor who provides their German voice — often for decades — ensuring continuity and a certain relationship to the stars for audiences.

But on Netflix, and perhaps elsewhere, many of those voices might be about to change.

Recently, Fröhlich and fellow voice actors Anne Helm (Margot Robbie) and Luise Helm (Scarlett Johansson) published a video on social media, letting their followers know they wouldn't provide their voices anymore.

Industry observers note that the reason? They refuse to sign Netflix's contract, seen by DW, which contains a clause that lets the American entertainment giant use their voices for training its AI.

Sources indicate that they're not the first voiceover artists to speak out on the topic. But they are the first ones to go viral.

"It was unexpected, completely," Fröhlich stated. "For whatever reason, we managed to reach people, perhaps because … we are three well-known women in the voiceover industry.".

In a recent development, "Over the years, we've managed to make good names for ourselves. It seems to have touched people that we made this statement together," she mentioned.

The newly introduced AI clause has been in Netflix's contracts since January 2026. Voice actors sign one ahead of every production. It was negotiated by BFFS, Germany's union for film and television actors.

In a recent development, fröhlich, like a significant number of voice actors, is not a member and feels as though the union went over their heads. However, BFFS says the deal gives them protection they wouldn't otherwise have.

Till Völger, an attorney and member of the union's board, says previous contracts and those with other streaming services are silent on AI or contain sweeping AI permissions.

Sources indicate that if an AI-generated voice doesn't sound like a particular person, companies are free to use the data they have gathered as they wish. Training can take place in other jurisdictions and may not require the actor's consent at all, he pointed out.

"We have a massive, massive protection gap," Völger told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that against that backdrop, BFFS argues the deal with Netflix is a step forward. It allows the firm to train its own systems with recordings, but voice actors must give separate, explicit consent before their recordings are used to create actual AI-generated voices, even if the voice isn't recognizable as theirs.

"We've created a contractual right that the law doesn't provide," remarked Völger. "Is the situation perfect? No. Is it better than before? Yes.".

It has been revealed that he would like to see other streaming services agree to the same conditions that Netflix has. In his view, only legislation could create the necessary protections voice actors are seeking.

Netflix says human performance "is and remains important to us," in statement provided to DW.

"In recent years, we have commissioned thousands of hours of German dubbing, and we intend to continue supporting a similar volume of work and the use of human voices," the statement continued.

Matti Klemm, the voice of Jason Momoa and beloved children's cartoon elephant Benjamin Blümchen, sees things differently. Like Fröhlich, he is refusing to sign the new contract.

"In short, it says: as soon as I record something for Netflix, I'm automatically training their AI, for free," he told DW. "My job is to create a German original, a dubbed version with my performance, not to train the computer systems of some tech companies.".

He is taking Netflix to court, backed by the Society for Civil Rights (GFF), to find out how his voice has been used for training in previous projects.

According to Davy Wang, who is coordinating the case for Klemm and GFF, the lawsuit will seek to stop Netflix using his recordings for training, disclose how previous data was used and establish whether Klemm is entitled to any damages.

Recent findings suggest that the suit will be filed at the end of the year or in early 2027. Supporters donated more than €50,000 to the legal fund in the first week following its announcement.

It has been revealed that for Klemm, what is at stake goes beyond training. "It's not about our voice, it's about our soul, our performance, the way we are," he said. "How far have we come when AI training matters more than my actual work?".

Netflix stated it cannot comment on a case that has not yet been filed.

For a multimillion-euro industry, the outcome of the case could reach well beyond Netflix and other companies and creative branches are watching. But no matter what the outcome of the lawsuit or contract agreements, voice actors' fears for their future run deep.

Those who don't sign contracts can't work, and streaming companies can make up a significant part of their income.

Recent findings suggest that "Many say: I've held out for 10 months, but I can't anymore. I have to sign this contract, I have to pay my rent, I have to feed my children," explained Fröhlich.

Beyond that, many fear the future of their industry and the connections they have formed with stars and audiences.

"For a many people I'm connected with Cameron Diaz and I evoke something within them," mentioned Fröhlich.

Recent findings suggest that but if Diaz is involved in more Netflix projects, "then I've basically lost her," she concluded. "I'll never be her voice again.".

#82016. A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s

A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1407 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A protein that helps protect the brain may offer scientists a promising latest way to fight Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
  • The findings, published in Science Advances by scientists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, suggest that strengthening the brain's own protective mechanisms could eventually lead to new treatments for neurodegenerative diseases.
  • The discovery is particularly significant because tau plays an essential role in keeping healthy brain cells functioning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A protein that helps protect the brain may offer scientists a promising latest way to fight Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Researchers have discovered that increasing levels of this protein can reduce the buildup of toxic tangles associated with brain damage, while also helping preserve the connections that allow nerve cells to communicate.

The findings, published in Science Advances by scientists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, suggest that strengthening the brain's own protective mechanisms could eventually lead to new treatments for neurodegenerative diseases. In experiments with mice, the researchers found that boosting the protein reduced several damaging changes associated with Alzheimer's, including brain shrinkage and the accumulation of abnormal tau proteins.

The discovery is particularly significant because tau plays an essential role in keeping healthy brain cells functioning. Under normal conditions, tau proteins help stabilize microtubules, tiny structures that provide internal support to neurons and help maintain the intricate networks of the nervous system.

In Alzheimer's and several related disorders, however, tau proteins can become abnormal and stick together, forming harmful clumps known as tau tangles. These tangles disrupt the normal functioning of nerve cells and are associated with cognitive decline and neuronal death. Diseases characterized by abnormal tau accumulation are collectively called tauopathies.

A Protective Protein With a Surprising Role in Alzheimer's.

The researchers investigated a protein called sorting-related receptor with A-type repeats (SORLA), which has already attracted scientific attention for its potential role in protecting the brain against Alzheimer's disease.

Recent findings suggest that previous studies have shown that SORLA can help limit the production and accumulation of amyloid-beta, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's. Amyloid-beta can build up into plaques in the brain, making it one of the disease's major pathological hallmarks alongside tau tangles.

"In the last 15 or 20 years, considerable data has come out from our lab and other groups showing that SORLA can suppress one of the hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease -- amyloid-beta generation and accumulation," stated Timothy Huang, PhD, assistant professor in the Center for Neurologic Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys.

"Very little was known, however, about whether SORLA affected the tau tangles reflected on the other side of the coin in Alzheimer's disease.".

It has been revealed that to investigate this question, the scientists developed a mouse model by breeding animals engineered to produce additional human SORLA with mice that develop tau tangles, brain atrophy, and cognitive impairments. This allowed them to examine whether higher SORLA levels could reduce tau accumulation and protect against the damage it causes.

Boosting SORLA Reduces Toxic Tau and Brain Shrinkage.

The results revealed that additional SORLA provided protection against several processes that contribute to tau tangles and the progression of neurodegenerative disease.

According to recent reports, one notable effect involved a process called hyperphosphorylation. This occurs when too many phosphate groups attach to tau proteins, altering their behavior and contributing to the development of harmful tangles. Higher SORLA levels reduced this abnormal modification.

The protein also limited the ability of misfolded tau to act as "seeds" that encourage other tau proteins to clump together. This seeding process can help toxic tau aggregates multiply and spread their damaging effects.

Sources indicate that beyond reducing tau abnormalities, SORLA helped preserve synapses, the specialized connections through which neurons communicate. It also protected synaptic plasticity, the brain's ability to strengthen or modify those connections, which is essential for learning, memory, and normal cognitive function.

"When you upregulate SORLA, you can suppress the negative effects found in tauopathies," remarked Huijie Huang, PhD, a staff scientist in the Huang lab at Sanford Burnham Prebys and lead author of the study.

"We found there was less brain atrophy and less tau accumulation, which was very exciting to see.".

Removing the Protein Makes Brain Damage Worse.

After observing the benefits of increasing SORLA, the researchers examined what would happen if the protein were missing entirely.

Industry observers note that SORLA is produced using instructions encoded by a gene called Sorl1. Some people carry mutations that interfere with this gene's function, potentially disrupting the production or activity of the protective protein.

To investigate the consequences, the team studied genetically modified mice that lacked Sorl1 and therefore could not produce SORLA.

It has been revealed that the results contrasted sharply with those seen in mice carrying additional copies of the protein. Instead of protecting against tau-related damage, the absence of SORLA made the harmful effects more severe.

"The opposite turned out to be true when we deleted the ability to produce SORLA proteins," remarked Tim Huang, senior and corresponding author of the manuscript. "A lack of SORLA exacerbated the harmful effects observed in tauopathies.".

These contrasting results provided further evidence that SORLA plays an important protective role in the brain and may influence how severely tau-related diseases progress.

A New Clue Could Lead to Alzheimer's Treatments.

To understand why changing SORLA levels had such different effects, the researchers examined the molecular activity of individual brain cells and the surrounding tissue.

They combined advanced sequencing methods to measure protein levels and gene activity in individual cells with techniques that map where RNA and proteins are located within brain tissue. This detailed approach helped reveal how SORLA influences the biological processes involved in neurodegeneration.

The analysis showed that increasing SORLA helped prevent harmful changes in protein production at synapses while also suppressing other mechanisms associated with tauopathy progression.

The researchers also discovered that higher SORLA levels reduced abnormal gene activity in glial cells. These cells perform several essential functions in the nervous system, including supporting, maintaining, and protecting neurons. Changes in glial cell activity can contribute to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases.

One finding was especially intriguing because it pointed toward a potential target for existing medications.

"One particularly notable finding that we can build on is the upregulation of a member of the plexin-B family of receptors in the absence of SORLA," noted Huijie Huang.

Plexin-B receptors are proteins involved in cellular signaling, helping cells respond to information from their surroundings. The increased activity of a receptor in this family when SORLA was absent suggests that this signaling pathway could be involved in some of the damaging changes associated with tau disorders.

Importantly, drugs capable of targeting this family of receptors already exist, raising the possibility that scientists could investigate whether they might be useful against tau-related dementia.

Recent findings suggest that "There are unique drugs that can target this class of receptors that we may be able to apply to tau-related dementia disorders," said Tim Huang. "One potential future direction is to repurpose these drugs to target overactivation of glial cells and perhaps reverse some of the phenotypes in tauopathies.".

The Next Step Toward Human Alzheimer's Research.

Although the findings are encouraging, the protective effects were demonstrated in mice, and more research is needed to determine how these mechanisms operate in humans.

The team now hopes to investigate how individual types of brain cells respond when SORLA levels increase or decrease. One planned approach involves transplanting human neurons or glial cells into mouse brains, allowing researchers to examine the effects of different SORLA mutations in a living brain affected by disease.

Recent findings suggest that "Mouse cells and human cells are different," mentioned Tim Huang. "Because we're looking at human disease, it's more informative if we can observe the modulation and dysfunction of SORLA in the context of a human cell inside of a diseased brain environment.".

These experiments could help clarify how SORLA protects neurons from toxic tau accumulation and why disruptions in its function make neurodegeneration worse.

Ultimately, the researchers hope that a deeper understanding of this protective protein will reveal fresh treatment strategies, either by enhancing SORLA's activity or by repurposing existing drugs to interfere with damaging cellular pathways. Such approaches could eventually offer new ways to combat Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia driven by toxic tau tangles.

The study was supported by the National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute and National Institute on Aging.

Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, vitamin C may do more than support everyday health.
  • Exposure to nitrates and nitrites has increased in North American diets over the past several decades.
  • One of these reactions, called nitrosation, can produce substances that researchers suspect may contribute to cancer development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, vitamin C may do more than support everyday health. New research from the University of Waterloo suggests that it could also help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming during digestion. Using mathematical modeling, scientists investigated how vitamin C influences chemical reactions in the digestive system that have been linked to cancer risk.

Exposure to nitrates and nitrites has increased in North American diets over the past several decades. These compounds are found in cured meats such as bacon and salami, as well as in fruits and vegetables grown in soil or water affected by pollution. Although nitrates and nitrites contribute to important functions in the brain and cardiovascular system, they can also participate in potentially harmful reactions once they reach the stomach.

One of these reactions, called nitrosation, can produce substances that researchers suspect may contribute to cancer development. Understanding what causes these chemicals to form, and what might prevent their formation, has been a longstanding challenge.

Why Vitamin C Could Change the Cancer Risk Equation.

According to recent reports, "Since at least the 90s, researchers have been studying the link between cancer and these compounds, with conflicting results," stated Dr. Gordon McNicol, a post-doctoral researcher in applied mathematics and the first author of the study. "Our work suggests that the presence of dietary Vitamin C may help explain these inconsistencies.".

Industry observers note that to investigate this possibility, the researchers developed a mathematical model that simulates how nitrates and nitrites travel through the body and undergo chemical changes. The model incorporated several interconnected systems, including the salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, and plasma, the liquid portion of blood.

Sources indicate that their simulations revealed that vitamin C consumed alongside nitrates and nitrites may interfere with the formation of potentially harmful compounds. This could help explain why foods containing nitrates do not necessarily carry the same risks.

For example, leafy vegetables such as spinach naturally contain both nitrates and vitamin C. According to the model, the presence of vitamin C could limit the chemical reactions associated with cancer risk, potentially helping explain the protective effects suggested by some dietary research.

Could Taking Vitamin C After Meals Help?

The researchers also explored whether vitamin C supplements might offer similar benefits when taken after eating.

Their findings suggest that taking vitamin C after each meal could moderately reduce the formation of nitrosation products associated with cancer risk. This effect could be particularly relevant when consuming foods containing nitrates and nitrites, including processed meats such as bacon and salami.

Recent findings suggest that however, the results come from mathematical simulations rather than clinical trials. Although the model predicts that vitamin C can reduce the production of potentially harmful chemicals, further research is needed to determine whether this translates into a measurable reduction in cancer risk in humans.

Latest Clues for Future Cancer Prevention Research.

In a recent development, the researchers believe their model could help scientists better understand the complicated relationship between diet, digestive chemistry, and cancer risk. It may also provide guidance for future experiments examining how nutritional choices influence the formation of potentially harmful compounds.

"This work provides a mechanistic roadmap for future clinical and laboratory studies by identifying the key interacting drivers of these potentially harmful chemical reactions, including nitrite exposure, antioxidant intake, meal timing, gastric conditions and oral microbiome activity," noted Dr. Anita Layton, professor of applied mathematics and Canada 150 researcher chair. "This model can help researchers design more targeted experiments and interventions, focusing on when and in whom nitrosation is most likely to occur.".

By identifying how factors such as vitamin C intake, meal timing, stomach conditions, and bacteria in the mouth interact, the model could help researchers develop more precise strategies for studying and potentially reducing cancer-related chemical reactions during digestion.

The study, "Vitamin C as a nitrosation inhibitor: A modelling study across dietary patterns and water quality," was published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology.

Erdogan's political fate may be determined by Turkey's Kurds

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1511 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Turkey’s persecuted pro-Kurdish party has emerged as a kingmaker in the country’s upcoming election, playing a decisive role that may just tip the balance enough to unseat two-decade ruler Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
  • In a key setback to the Turkish president and leader of the Justice and Development Party (AK Party), the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) last month confirmed that it would not put forward its own presidential candidate, a move analysts say allows its supporters to vote for Erdogan’s main rival.
  • Recent findings suggest that “We are facing a turning point that will shape the future of Turkey and (its) society,” noted the HDP in a statement on March 23.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turkey’s persecuted pro-Kurdish party has emerged as a kingmaker in the country’s upcoming election, playing a decisive role that may just tip the balance enough to unseat two-decade ruler Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

In a key setback to the Turkish president and leader of the Justice and Development Party (AK Party), the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) last month confirmed that it would not put forward its own presidential candidate, a move analysts say allows its supporters to vote for Erdogan’s main rival.

Recent findings suggest that “We are facing a turning point that will shape the future of Turkey and (its) society,” noted the HDP in a statement on March 23. “To fulfill our historical responsibility against the one-man rule, we will not field a presidential candidate in (the) May 14 elections.”.

It has been revealed that it is a twist of irony for the Turkish strongman, who spent the better half of the past decade cracking down on the party after it began chipping away at his voter base. Its former leader Selahattin Demirtas has been in prison for nearly seven years and the party faces possible closure by a court for suspected collusion with the militant Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and affiliated groups. But its influence may nonetheless determine the course of Turkey’s politics.

Sources indicate that the HDP’s decision not to field a candidate came just three days after head of the Republican People’s Party (CHP) Kemal Kilicdaroglu, Erdogan’s main rival, visited the party’s co-chairs. He told reporters that the solution to Turkey’s problems, “including the Kurdish problem” lies in parliament,” according to Turkish media.

Sources indicate that kilicdaroglu, who represents the six-party Nation Alliance opposition bloc, is the strongest contender to run against Erdogan in years. And while the HDP hasn’t yet unveiled whether it will put its weight behind him, analysts say it is the kingmaker in the elections.

Erdogan's 'polar opposite' wants to replace him as president of Turkey.

Industry observers note that “It was a carefully crafted political discourse,” Hisyar Ozsoy, deputy co-chair of the HDP and a member of parliament from the predominantly Kurdish province of Diyarbakir, told CNN. “We are not going to have our own candidate, and we will leave it to the international community to interpret it the way they wish.”.

Experts say the crackdown on the HDP is rooted in the threat it poses to Erdogan politically, as well as its position as one of the main parties representing Turkey’s Kurds, an ethnic minority from which a separatist militant movement has emerged.

The party and the Kurdish people have had a complicated relationship with Erdogan. The leader courted the Kurds in earlier years by granting them more rights and reversing restrictions on the use of their language. Relations with the HDP were also cordial once, as Erdogan worked with the party on a brief peace process with the PKK.

But ties between Erdogan and the HDP later turned sour, and the HDP fell under a sweeping crackdown aimed at the PKK and their affiliates.

Kurds are the biggest minority in Turkey, making up between 15% and 20% of the population, according to Minority Rights Group International.

It is unclear if the HDP will endorse Kilicdaroglu, but analysts say that the deliberate distance may be beneficial for the opposition candidate.

Sources indicate that the accusations against the HDP place it in a precarious position during the elections. It currently faces a case in Turkey’s Constitutional Court over suspected ties to the PKK, which is designated as a terrorist group by Turkey, the United States and the European Union. Knowing it may be banned at any moment, its candidates are running under the Green Left Party in parliament.

If the opposition is seen as allying with the HDP, Erdogan’s AK Party may use its influence in the media to discredit it as being pro-PKK, said Murat Somer, a political science professor at Koc University in Istanbul and author of Return to Point Zero, a book on the Turkish-Kurdish question in Turkey.

In a recent development, the HDP’s threat to Erdogan’s hold on power became apparent after the June 2015 election, the first general election it participated in. It won 13% of the seats, denying the ruling AK Party its majority for the first time since 2002. Erdogan, however, called a snap election five months later, which led to a drop in the HDP’s support to 10.7%, as well as the restoration of the AK Party’s overall majority.

Recent findings suggest that “They are a kingmaker in these elections because the HDP gets about half of the votes of the Kurdish population in Turkey,” noted Somer, adding that the other, more conservative Kurdish voters have traditionally voted for Erdogan’s AK Party. And last month, the Free Cause Party (HUDA-PAR), a tiny Kurdish-Islamist party announced support for Erdogan in the elections. The party has never won seats in parliament.

Erdogan's political fate may rest on his response to the earthquake.

The HDP knows that its position is key to the outcome of next month’s vote, but that it’s also in a delicate situation.

“We want to play the game wisely, and we need to be very careful,” said Ozsoy, adding that the party wants to avoid a “contaminated political climate” where the elections are polarized “between a very ugly ultra-nationalist discourse against Kilicdaroglu and others.”.

The party was founded in 2012 with a number of aims, remarked Ozsoy, one of which was “peaceful and democratic resolution of the Kurdish conflict.”.

Somer mentioned that the party was seen to be “an initiative” of the PKK, which later led to a heavy government crackdown on it in the name of counterterrorism.

Its former leader Demirtas remains an influential figure.

The Turkish government has been trying to link the HDP to the PKK but has so far failed to prove “a real connection,” noted Asli Aydintasbas, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution in Washington, DC.

A post-Erdogan Turkey may give some breathing space to the Kurds and Kurdish-dominated parties in Turkey, Aydintasbas told CNN, noting that many Kurdish voters have recently left Erdogan’s camp. “For HDP, this is more than just an ideological choice,” she said. “It’s a matter of survival.”.

Ozsoy claims his party understands what’s at stake, not only for Turkey’s Kurds but for all its minorities.

It has been revealed that “We are aware of our responsibility here. We are aware of our role. We know we are in a kingmaker position,” the HDP lawmaker mentioned.

Two women arrested for not wearing hijab following ‘yogurt attack’.

Oil prices surge after OPEC+ producers announce surprise cuts.

Oil prices spiked Monday after OPEC+ producers unexpectedly announced that they would cut output. Brent crude, the global benchmark, jumped 5.31% to $84.13 a barrel, while WTI, the US benchmark, rose 5.48% to $79.83. Both were the sharpest price rises in almost a year. The collective output cut by the nine members of OPEC+ totals 1.66 million barrels per day.

Iran blames Israel for the killing of second IRGC officer, vows to respond.

A second Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) officer died following an attack in Syria on Friday, according to Iranian state media on Sunday. Iranian state media said the Iranian military adviser died after an Israeli attack near the Syrian capital Damascus left him wounded. The attack also killed another IRGC officer. In a tweet on Sunday, Iranian government spokesman Ali Bahadori Jahromi said the alleged Israeli attack wouldn’t go unanswered. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Nasser Kanaani said on Sunday that Iran has the right to respond to “state terrorism.”.

Iranian-American comedian Maz Jobrani, who has been touring the Middle East, spoke to CNN’s Becky Anderson about his support for the protests in his homeland, saying that he used his standup comedy platform to highlight the “brutality against the Iranian people.”.

“It was an opportunity for me to say, ‘let’s keep fighting,’” he stated.

An Iranian state news outlet is gloating at what it sees as the demise of the US dollar.

IRNA recreated a popular meme to mark China and Brazil’s decision to reportedly ditch the US dollar as an intermediary in trade, citing the Chinese state news outlet, China Daily. It shows two men representing China and Brazil posing in front of a grave labelled “USD.”.

In a recent development, the meme was pinned to the top of IRNA’s Twitter page, and was met with laughter and ridicule. “Dream on,” noted another user, pointing to the dollar’s use as the main reserve currency around the world.

China Daily noted that the agreement was part of “the rising global use of the Chinese renminbi.” It would reportedly enable China and Brazil to conduct trade and financial transactions using local currencies instead of the dollar.

A bright light in Hollywood has gone dim.

In a recent development, broadway star Steven Hack, who also had minor roles in American Horror Story and Seinfeld, has died after suffering a medical emergency, Los Angeles’ Interact Theatre Manufacturer confirmed. He was 68.

According to recent reports, “It is with great sadness that we share the news that Steven Hack, a founding member of Interact Theatre Company, recently passed away at home following a sudden and unexpected cardiac event,” the company wrote in a recent statement shared to Instagram. “Steven was a gifted and versatile performer, a superb graphic artist, and a cherished member of our artistic family.”.

Hack died of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, according to the County of Los Angeles Medical Examiner, a condition caused by plaque buildup in the arterial walls, per the America Heart Association.

“His creativity and talent helped shape Interact in its earliest years,” the statement continued, “and his artistry, humor, warmth, and generous spirit enriched everything he touched.”.

Industry observers note that hack was born in St. Louis in 1958 before going on to study at the California Institute of the Arts and the American Academy of Dramatic Arts.

“Steven took great pride in his early career as a Broadway dancer, which included performing in the original production of CATS and touring with A Chorus Line,” Interact Theatre Company noted. “Here in Los Angeles, he went on to work extensively in film, television, and commercials.”.

In fact, he made his screen debut as one of the teenage dancers in the 1978 film Grease before landing roles in other films like Fantastic Four, Thor: The Dark World and The Happytime Murders.

He also dominated the small screen with credits in American Horror Story: 1984, Marvel’s Agent Carter, Criminal Minds, The Newsroom, Days of Our Lives, The West Wing, Scrubs, General Hospital, Seinfeld and so many more.

“As we remember Steven, we celebrate not only his many contributions to our manufacturer, but also the joy of knowing and working with him,” Interact Theatre Company wrote. “He will always hold a special place in Interact’s history and in the hearts of those who knew him.”.

They expressed hope that Hack’s "memory be a blessing,” adding, "We extend our heartfelt condolences to his family, friends, and all who loved him.”.

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that emerging research suggests that biological sex and genetics may play a major role in how neurological disorders develop, progress, and respond to treatment.
  • Sources indicate that researchers are increasingly finding that certain neurological conditions can behave differently depending on a person's biological sex and genetic makeup.
  • Two of the new studies highlight how menopause and inherited genetic factors may influence Alzheimer's vulnerability and treatment responses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that emerging research suggests that biological sex and genetics may play a major role in how neurological disorders develop, progress, and respond to treatment. The findings, which will be presented at Neuroscience 2026, reveal important differences that could help researchers develop more personalized approaches to treating complex brain conditions. Neuroscience 2026 is the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and the world's largest source of emerging news about brain science and health.

Sources indicate that researchers are increasingly finding that certain neurological conditions can behave differently depending on a person's biological sex and genetic makeup. Understanding these differences could lead to treatments better suited to each individual's biology. Two conditions receiving particular attention are Alzheimer's disease (AD), an incurable disorder that progressively damages memory and other brain functions, and fibromyalgia, a chronic illness marked by persistent pain and fatigue that affects 2-4% of the global population. According to the World Health Organization, Alzheimer's affects between 35 and 40 million people worldwide.

Menopause, Genetics, and Alzheimer's Disease.

Two of the new studies highlight how menopause and inherited genetic factors may influence Alzheimer's vulnerability and treatment responses.

One investigation found that people carrying genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's responded differently to menopause hormone therapy (MHT) compared with those without the same genetic risks. The effects also varied according to the particular combination of hormones used. These findings suggest that both genetic background and hormone therapy formulation deserve consideration when evaluating treatment options. (Mateja Perović, University of Toronto).

A separate study examined rodents undergoing menopause that also carried genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's. Researchers observed that brain circuits responsible for memory became particularly vulnerable, providing evidence that menopause may represent an important period of increased susceptibility for women who are genetically predisposed to the disease. (Stephanie M. Perez, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio).

Sex Differences in Chronic Pain and Brain Inflammation.

The other two studies explored how biological sex influences pain sensitivity, immune activity, and the effects of inflammation on the brain.

In a recent development, in a mouse model of fibromyalgia, females continued to show heightened sensitivity to touch and stronger immune system activation compared with males. The findings suggest that the biological processes contributing to chronic pain may differ between sexes, potentially making treatments tailored to these differences more effective. (Yasmin Sahlloul, University of Cincinnati).

It has been revealed that another investigation uncovered differences in how prolonged intestinal inflammation influences the brain. Using a mouse model, researchers found that chronic gut inflammation affected brain function and Alzheimer's related disease changes differently in males and females. The results provide additional evidence that biological sex may influence the relationship between inflammation and neurological disease. (Nurcan Kilic, University of North Dakota).

Toward More Personalized Treatments for Brain Disorders.

Recent findings suggest that together, the four studies underscore the importance of examining sex and genetic differences when investigating neurological conditions. By identifying biological factors that influence disease progression and treatment responses, researchers hope to move toward more precise therapies for Alzheimer's, fibromyalgia, and other difficult-to-treat brain disorders.

Industry observers note that "These four studies illustrate the fascinating discoveries that can be made when focusing on female-specific biology or possible sex differences in AD-related symptoms and risk factors," said Liisa Galea, PhD, Treliving Family Chair in Women's Mental Health at Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and moderator of the press conference. "The research presented at Neuroscience 2026 helps us pinpoint the specific differences that may help us develop more targeted treatment using precision approaches, even for some of our most complex brain disorders.".

This projector is a handy, budget-priced tool for educating young stargazers, especially when it comes to teaching them about constellations. It’s easy to use and offers excellent image quality for its size — it’s just disappointing the selection of slides is so limited.

Requires three AA batteries (not included).

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

I didn’t expect much as I unboxed the Brainstorm Night Sky; after all, I’m significantly older than this educational star projector’s target audience. Perhaps I’d come away with a sense of wonder and delight, coupled with mild irritation at having to hunt down three AA batteries to power it.

According to recent reports, instead, I was filled with envy as the Brainstorm Night Sky reminded me just what I was missing, thanks to the rigors of light pollution. A few minutes after powering it down, I was already making plans for my first dark sky trip, yearning for a view that rivaled the Brainstorm’s cosmic images.

Recent findings suggest that draw the curtains, press the Night Sky’s single button (tilting the projector and twisting the focus as appropriate) and it projects a circular image onto a ceiling or wall. Press the button again and the projection slowly begins to rotate, slowly but stutter-free. It really is that simple to operate and, aimed at budding astronomers aged eight or above, it's reasonably lightweight without feeling flimsy.

Weight: 14.8 oz (420 g)Bulb type: Non-specifiedLaser: NoControl: On-unitRotation: Yes, one speedProjection area: Up to 8.2 ft (2.5 m)Sleep timer: Yes (30 mins)Power: 3x AA batteries Speaker: No.

I was initially a little surprised by the size of the projection: at up to 8.2 feet (2.5 m) wide it’s not going to fill an entire ceiling. It also switches off after 30 minutes, a limit that can’t be disabled, so if you’re looking to put on your own space-themed party this is not the projector for you. But it’s on point for home education and, priced from $49.99, the Brainstorm Night Sky projector won’t break the bank.

Sources indicate that there’s minimal distortion around the edge of the images; the planets are spherical from the word go, unlike some projectors where I’ve had to tweak them to stop Mars turning into an egg. And I never once had to crane my neck because half the solar system had been projected onto a bookcase.

The Brainstorm Night Sky model I tested comes with four slides, each with a case to protect them from smudges and sticky fingers. You place one into the provided slide housing then insert that into the projector. There’s the moon, the solar system, and two showing the Northern Hemisphere’s night sky, as seen from Hawaii (a key location for astronomy).

I can appreciate the educational value of the first couple, even if I am still seething at Pluto being demoted back in 2006. But it was the latter pair of slides that really opened my eyes to what I could be seeing over my head.

I can spot maybe 10-20 stars from my backyard, cloud cover permitting; thanks to light pollution, that’s it. Even though the best stargazing apps can show me what I should see, when I step outside, all I typically see with the naked eye is the odd pinprick in the void.

It has been revealed that but as soon as I inserted that third slide, a striking stellar display appeared above my head, with more stars than I could hope to count. Even knowing that Hawaii’s night sky stretches far further than eight feet across, the difference between this view and the one from my house was like night and day. Brainstorm claims this slide features over 20,000 stars, though that’s likely referring to the source photo rather than the projected image.

Sources indicate that the fourth slide — the same crisp starscape but with every visible constellation labelled — was almost as attention-grabbing. Educational value aside, it drove home that I couldn’t see the majority of these star patterns to name them, my local night sky is that polluted.

Recent findings suggest that knowing what I was missing out on made me determined to take my stargazing further afield. Some of the best smart telescopes can lessen the impact of light pollution, but stepping away from skyglow is the most effective option. Hawaii’s a little far to travel, but I’ve already started looking into local dark sky sites. I just need to grab a pair of the best binoculars for stargazing, hop on my bike and I’m ready to go.

Industry observers note that the Brainstorm Night Sky’s projections are crisp enough that you can easily make out every constellation name, but they could be a hair brighter. The Ainael Meter Galaxy Projector, for example, delivers more illumination.

If you want to use the Brainstorm Night Sky to relax, the rotate function gives its projections an oddly hypnotic effect, and the device is whisper-quiet to boot. And while Brainstorm doesn’t specify battery life, one set of rechargeables lasted me for several days.

Unfortunately, the Brainstorm Night Sky's slide collection is a little limited. There are two models, a blue version with four slides (the one I tested) and a gray version with six slides (featuring additional space shuttle and black hole images). The included instructions state you can purchase an additional slide disc showing the Southern Hemisphere’s stars, but that’s a maximum of seven images. Nor is this projector compatible with the slides from the Brainstorm Deep Sky Projector.

Industry observers note that it’s a little disappointing given that Brainstorm has clearly put thought into the projector’s educational value. Those instructions double as a poster of the solar system, and children can use a “secret code” (printed on the instructions) to explore more astronomy facts on the manufacturer’s website.

Offering extra slide packs, of the kind you can buy for the Pococo Galaxy Projector, would give it more long-term appeal. As is, I can see its novelty and educational value diminishing over time, at which point you can upgrade to one of the best star projectors.

It has been revealed that if you’re not bothered by the lack of expandability, the Brainstorm Night Sky’s price, image quality and ease of use still make it a useful tool for kindling a child’s interest in astronomy, or as a budget-friendly gift for junior stargazers. It’s certainly spurred me into action — how much is a plane ticket to Hawaii, anyway?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that as of Tuesday, Nov.
  • If you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Imbrium and Crisium, as well as the Copernicus Crater.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Full Moon is here, and this one's a Supermoon. That means the Moon is closer to Earth than usual, making it appear slightly bigger and brighter in the night sky.

Industry observers note that as of Tuesday, Nov. 24, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Full Moon phase, with 100% of its surface visible.

If you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Imbrium and Crisium, as well as the Copernicus Crater. With binoculars, you'll also see the Archimedes Crater, the Endymion Crater, and the Alphonsus Crater. And if you have a telescope, you'll get to see all this plus the Apollo 15 landing spot, the Schiller Crater, and the Rima Hyginus.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

It takes around 29.5 days for the Moon to move through all its phases, according to NASA. Throughout this period, the Moon's position relative to Earth and the Sun determines how much of its illuminated surface we can see. Starting with a Fresh Moon, the visible portion gradually increases until it reaches a Full Moon, before shrinking again as the cycle comes back around.

Latest Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere).

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

Nick Carter Ordered to Stand Trial on Sexual Assault Claims From Dream Singer Melissa Schuman

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A judge has decided to hold a trial in the sexual assault lawsuit brought against Backstreet Boys member Nick Carter by Melissa Schuman, a former member of the teen-pop group Dream.
  • 23) court ruling, obtained by Billboard, says there “is a triable issue of material fact” as to whether Carter forced Schuman to have sex when they were co-starring in the teen horror movie The Hollow in 2003.
  • It has been revealed that schuman sued Carter in 2023 under California’s Sexual Abuse and Cover-Up Accountability Act, a state law that temporarily lifted the statute of limitations for otherwise-expired sex assault claims.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A judge has decided to hold a trial in the sexual assault lawsuit brought against Backstreet Boys member Nick Carter by Melissa Schuman, a former member of the teen-pop group Dream.

A Monday (Nov. 23) court ruling, obtained by Billboard, says there “is a triable issue of material fact” as to whether Carter forced Schuman to have sex when they were co-starring in the teen horror movie The Hollow in 2003. A trial is set for May 2027 in Santa Monica, Calif.

It has been revealed that schuman sued Carter in 2023 under California’s Sexual Abuse and Cover-Up Accountability Act, a state law that temporarily lifted the statute of limitations for otherwise-expired sex assault claims. Under that law, claims only qualified for revival if there was an allegation that some business entity had conspired to “cover up” a prior sexual assault by the same perpetrator.

It has been revealed that carter vehemently denies Schuman’s sexual battery claim and has countersued her, as well as various other sexual assault accusers, for defamation. His lawyers argued that Schuman’s case had a fatal defect: she failed to allege the right kind of cover-up, meaning it was not eligible for California’s 2023 claim revival window.

It has been revealed that however, California passed another law last year, called the Justice for Survivors of Sexual Assault Act, that opened another two-year window for sexual assault claims with looser cover-up requirements. Judge Lisa K. Sepe-Wiesenfeld ruled Monday that this second law can be successfully used to revive Schuman’s claims.

“The individual claim against defendant Carter for sexual battery is proper irrespective of the existence of a cover up,” wrote the judge. “Defendants cannot prevail on summary adjudication merely by attacking the cover-up allegations.”.

According to recent reports, the question at this stage, then, is merely whether there’s enough conflicting evidence in the case to go to a jury. Judge Sepe-Wiesenfeld believes the answer is yes, since Schuman has remarked that Carter assaulted her, while the singer said it never happened.

“There is a conflict in the evidence presented as to whether a sexual assault of Plaintiff occurred,” wrote the judge.

A lawyer for Schuman, Jamie Majerus, tells Billboard that Monday’s ruling “reflects the existence of substantial factual disputes that must be resolved by a jury.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Among the evidence before the Court is sworn testimony from Carter’s own sister, who testified he had sex with a 15-year-old, and testimony from his best friend at the time, describing repeated episodes of extreme alcohol consumption, including drinking an entire bottle of tequila at a time and forcing himself to vomit afterward,” noted Majerus. “A jury, not the defense, will decide what weight to give that evidence.”.

Carter’s lawyers did not immediately return a request for comment on Tuesday (Nov. 24).

It has been revealed that the Backstreet Boys member has faced various public accusations of sexual assault over the last decade, all of which he denies. He’s been sued by three other women in addition to Schuman: Shannon Ruth, Ashley Repp and Laura Penly. Carter is currently scheduled to go to trial on those claims next August in Las Vegas.
